paragraphs.text: Muhammad Hashim Khan Kakar, J. The petitioner, Waris Masih, was convicted section 302(b) PPC and sentenced to death by the Trial for the murder of his wife, Mst. Jamila Bibi. He was also convicted section 337-A(ii) PPC for causing to his minor children sentenced to undergo one year R.I. as Tazir with an order to pay Arsh @ 5% of the Diyat to the injured. Against his convictions and sentences, he preferred an appeal before the Islamabad High Court, Islamabad was dismissed vide impugned judgment dated 10.10.2018, however, only sentence reduced imprisonment for life. Being aggrieved, the petitioner now approached this Court by filing the instant jail petition.

The facts of the case, as enumerated in the impugned judgment the High Court, are that: “2. As per the complaint (Exh.PM), Jangi Masih, father of Mst. Jamila Bibi/deceased, alleged that his daughter Mst. Jamila Bibi was married to the appellant/Waris Masih 15 years ago and they J, P. No. 787/2018. have six children, whereas the appellant/Waris Masih is a drug addict, who always used to quarrel with Mst. Jamila Bibi. On 06.07.2015 in the midnight, the appellant/Waris Masih assaulted wife Mst. Jamila Bibi and two minors Rimsha Bibi Ramesh by inflicting Dhandas blows. As a result, whereof, Mst. Jamila Bibi succumbed to injuries, whereas minors got seriously injured. The main dispute referred in the complaint is a family dispute between the appellant/Waris Masih and Mst. Jamila Bibi/deceased. After formal Investigation, a report U/S 173 Cr.P.C. was submitted before the learned trial Court, charge been framed, the appellant/Waris Masih pleaded not guilty, on the prosecution produced 10 PWs, and the appellant/Waris Masih recorded his statement U/S 342 Cr.P.C. On conclusion arguments, the learned trial convicted appellant /Waris Masih and sentenced him U/S 302-B PPC to death as Tazir along with the fine and he was also convicted U/S 337-A(ii) PPC to one year R.I.”

We have heard the learned counsels for the parties gone through the record in depth. In order to avoid unnecessary repetition, we have incorporated and addressed the submissions and contentions raised during the course of arguments throughout the ensuing discussion and analysis within this judgment. Though it is uncommon to obtain and present direct evidence in cases involving the death of women within their homes due to domestic violence, however, in the present case, such evidence has been provided by an injured witness, namely, Rimsha Waris Masih (PW-4), who is not only an injured witness but also biological daughter of the petitioner. She is, unquestionably, the inmate of the house in question where the incident occurred; therefore, her presence cannot be questioned in any way. She has pointed her accusatory fingers solely at the petitioner, holding him responsible for causing to her mother and sibling.

In accord this ocular account, Dr. Farrah Mazhar (PW-9) provided the medical evidence to the effect that she conducted a post- mortem examination on the deceased, Mst. Jamila Bibi, at 10 a.m. on 07.07.2015. In her opinion, the vital organs of the cranium were depressed due to bone degeneration. The probable duration between the injuries and 16 hours, while the time between the death and the postmortem examination was 17 hours. In the same vein, Dr. Tanveer Afsar Malik (PW-2) conducted an examination of Rimsha Bibi and Ramesh Masih, who sustained injuries, at Poly Clinic Hospital Islamabad on 06.07.2015. The medical completely corroborates the ocular account. o. In instances of domestic violence, particularly in the event homicidal of a wife in home of her husband, latter significantly responsible for providing a satisfactory circumstances that led to the tragedy within the scope of Article Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984 (“the Order”). The conduct of an accused before, during and after a crime is also relevant under Article 22 of the Order. In the same vein, Article 129 of the Order authorizes the Court infer adverse inferences from failure of party to submit evidence that it is capable of submitting. It is stated that the Court may assume evidence that could be produced but is not would be unfavorable to the individual who withholds it if it were produced. The principle concerning facts peculiarly within knowledge of accused is not unique to our jurisdiction rather it is followed universally. As-per well recognized legal encyclopedia of American law i.e. Corpus Juris Secundum, § 571, Volume 224A, the accused has the burden of proof as to a negative averment in the indictment, or a fact relied on as justification or excuse, where the subject matter thereof lies peculiarly within his knowledge. Similarly, section 106 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 contains similar provisions.

We are conscious of the settled principle of criminal jurisprudence that the burden of proving the commission of an offence rests squarely upon the prosecution, which must establish the guilt of the accused doubt. In this regard Article 117 of the Order embodies settled rule. Consequently, in cases of homicide, it is the sole responsibility of the prosecution to prove not only that a murder has been committed but also who committed said offence, through legally admissible and credible evidence. Where the prosecution fails to discharge this burden, the benefit of such doubt must, as a matter of right, be extended to the accused being a cornerstone of criminal justice and a fundamental safeguard against wrongful conviction.

It is worth mentioning where a wife is found dead home, the first and foundational question for determination is the nature of the death, namely, whether it was natural or unnatural. Once succeeds in establishing unnatural, the next question is whether the death was the result of suicide or homicide. Upon a finding that the death was homicide in nature, focus of investigation necessarily turns to the circumstances surrounding the occurrence, particularly the place of occurrence. At this juncture, it becomes necessary to distinguish between the concepts of burden of proof and onus of proof, which though related, operate in distinct legal spheres. The burden of proof refers to the obligation to establish the entire case and the guilt of the accused doubt, a burden which, in criminal proceedings, always rests upon the prosecution and never shifts. The onus of proof, on the other hand, pertains to the responsibility proving a particular fact or issue, may, depending upon circumstances of the case, shift during the course of trial.

In light of the aforementioned principles, the record would indicate that the petitioner denied the circumstances that were presented to him during his examination section 342 Cr.P.C., as indicated by the presented by the prosecution. He declined to present any evidence or provide a statement oath. The instant case abundantly establishes the fact that the death was caused by an act of causing injuries deceased’s cranium. petitioner maintained silence throughout the entire trial. The record shows that the petitioner and the deceased, as well as their children, were living in the same residence. wife of the petitioner passed away in an unnatural manner; however, he did not provide any information regarding the circumstances that led to her death. He must have provided an explanation of the events transpired at that time. In this regard, reference can be made to a decision of the Indian Supreme Court in the case of State of Andhra Pradesh v Gangula Satya Murthy (AIR 1997 SC 1588) wherein it deemed a failure offer an explanation as adverse to the accused by observing as under: “The fact that body of (Satya Vani) was found on the cot inside house of the respondent is a very telling circumstance against him. Respondent owed a duty to explain as to how a dead body which was resultant of a homicide happened to be in his house. In the absence of any such explanation from him the implication said circumstance is definitely adverse to the respondent.”

In cases of homicidal of a wife within the dwelling house, accused required provide a plausible for circumstances, particularly own conduct, as per Article Order, as the facts are “especially within the knowledge” of the accused. The absence of any substantiation in his mere denial under section 342 Cr.P.C. is entirely insufficient. A strong adverse inference can be drawn against him under Article 129(g) of the Order due to his failure to provide any explanation. We are aware that the prosecution is not relieved of the primary burden by Article Order, absence or falsity of explanation in the statement section 342 Cr.P.C. can only be used an additional circumstance when has established the other circumstances, which led to the sole conclusion of guilt of the accused. In the event that the prosecution successfully leads evidence to demonstrate that the accused and deceased were living together and were seen together shortly before the commission of the crime, or the offense occurs in the residence, and the husband fails to provide an explanation for how the deceased sustained or provides an explanation that is later discovered to be false, it serves as an additional link in the chain of circumstances against him. In this regard we are fortified by a judgment of this Court in the case of Saeed Ahmed v State (2015 SCMR 710) wherein it was held as under: “14. That with regard to vulnerable members of society, such as children, women and the infirm, who were living with the accused or were last in company accused ought to offer some explanation of what happened to them. If instead he remains silent or offers a false explanation he casts a shadow upon himself. This does not mean that the burden of proof has shifted onto the accused as it is for the prosecution to prove its case, however, in respect of the helpless or the weak that require protection or care it would not be sufficient for the accused to stay silent in circumstances tend to incriminate him, and if he elects to do so he lightens the burden of the prosecution. Article Qanun-e-Shahadat Order too stipulates that if a particular fact is especially within the knowledge of any person the burden of proving that fact is upon him. In the present case the prosecution had established its case against the appellant; two eye-witnesses had deposed against him and the medical evidence confirmed strangulation of the deceased. The appellant did not attend to the last rites of his wife who had died whilst residing with him, he also did not inform the police nor took his wife to a hospital disappeared for two months, such circumstances corroborate the prosecution case in the absence of the appellant offering a reasonable for his unnatural conduct.”

In the event of a homicidal of a wife within the residence, the victim was the accused’s wife who resided with him, the accused obligated to provide an explanation for the injuries the deceased sustained while residing in the same domicile house with him, as the deceased was discovered with multiple injuries and the cause of death was physical assault. The legal repercussions of this omission served as an additional link in the chain of circumstances in the absence of such an explanation.

The rationale for treating the husband as a primary suspect in cases where a wife suffers a homicidal within the matrimonial home is not only rooted in presumption of guilt, but also in the social, legal and moral position traditionally ascribed to the cement within the family unit. The family has long been recognized across civilization and legal systems the basic unit of society, and within this unit, the husband has historically been regarded as the head, manager and protector of the household. Classical legal and moral traditions, both religious secular, have consistently placed upon the male head of the family a heightened duty of care, supervision, and protection towards his spouse and dependents. Islamic jurisprudence articulates this responsibility with particular clarity. Verse of Surah An-Nisa Holy Qur’an states that, “Men caretakers of women.” The term qawwam in Arabic denotes one who bears responsibility, manages affairs and ensures protection and maintenance. In this sense, the husband is not merely a spouse, but a guardian of the family structure, entrusted with safeguarding its member.

The cases of Nasrullah v State (2017 SCMR 724) and Nazir Ahmed State (2018 SCMR 787) are frequently cited as a point of deviation for the proposition a husband cannot be convicted merely because the wife is found dead the matrimonial home. The rationale of the said judgements is firmly rooted in the settled principle that the burden of proof in criminal cases rests upon the prosecution and does not shift to the accused merely by reason of material proximity. However, a careful reading of the judgements reveal that the acquittals therein were not founded upon an absolute rejection of circumstantial reasoning in such cases, but rather upon the peculiar and fragile evidentiary matrix presented before the court. Even otherwise, ratio aforesaid cases cannot be mechanically extended to all cases involving the homicidal of a wife within the matrimonial home. In cases where there is no ocular account, no credible of third-party intervention, and where the death occurs within the exclusive domain of the matrimonial household, evidentiary landscape materially differs. In such _ situations, case rests upon strong consistent evidence, including the place of occurrence, last seen circumstances, conduct of the accused and failure to offer a plausible explanation for facts within his special knowledge. Where these circumstances collectively form a complete and unbroken chain, pointing irresistibly towards the guilt of the accused and excluding every reasonable hypothesis of innocence, reliance upon circumstantial evidence cannot be said to be unsafe.

It would also not be out of place to mention father classical criminology generally considered to be the Italian nobleman professor of law, Cesare Bonesana, Marchese di Beccaria who in 1764 published Dei Delitti e della pene (On Crimes and Punishment) states that: “There are some crimes which are, at the same time, of frequent occurrence in society, yet difficult proof, [...] legislator, instead of increasing the punishment, which would only serve to multiply the number of criminals, should endeavor facilitate the proof of the crime.” Beccaria warns if society relies only on torture or extreme presumptions to “solve” crimes taken place in secrecy, it breeds nothing use to serve justice. But if the law intelligently shifts the evidentiary playing field (e.g., requiring the person special access to explain), Justice can become deterrent. Hence this principle can be applied on such cases as the crime took place in secrecy of home which is in custody of husband as this is a classic “crime of difficult proof and hence he cannot be given a clean chit to go free without offering at least some plausible for the unfortunate event that occurred.

Considering produced by _ the in the light of above-mentioned principles of criminal jurisprudence, the sequence of circumstances is entirely consistent the hypothesis that the petitioner committed the murder of the deceased. These circumstances wholly inconsistent theory of an unknown intruder or the petitioner’s innocence. The cascade of guilt that results from the non-participation of the petitioner in the burial rites, failure to report the crime, abscondence immediately after the occurrence until arrest, the unnatural deceased home, and the petitioner and deceased being the only adults in the house at the time of the occurrence leaves no room for any inference other than the petitioner’s involvement in the murder.

Trial Appellate meticulously examined and ocular and correctly determined petitioner’s culpability was established doubt. We have not identified any errors in the application of law or the evaluation evidence. conviction substantiated by a strong chain and oral evidence.
For what been discussed above, we cannot take any exception to the impugned judgment of the High Court which is accordingly upheld and, consequently, this petition is dismissed and leave is refused.

Before parting the judgment in hand, it is important to note women, equal members society, deserve unwavering protection, respect and dignity within the sanctity of their residences. Their relationship with males as mothers, sisters, wives and daughters held in the highest regard, and it is imperative that no one be permitted to contaminate or undermine this sacred bond. We have observed in numerous instances women treated extreme cruelty, sometimes compared to being “hunted like animals” over petty matters. This type of brutality is especially evident when spouses are struggling with drug addiction. It is imperative that the State take decisive action by implementing comprehensive legislation, enforcement mechanisms supportive programs to halt this cruelty and safeguard most vulnerable members of society. This must be done in accordance with the constitutional obligations outlined in Article 9 (right to life and liberty) and Article 25 (equality) of the Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan. ISLAMABAD 21.01.2026 (Farrukh) Approved for Reporting
